One strategy to address the scarcity of fossil fuel energy sources is to conduct research and development aimed at improving fuel consumption efficiency. The development for fuel efficiency involves optimizing the engine management system, particularly the ignition system, so that the fuel entering the combustion chamber can burn completely. This study employs an experimental method by modifying the installation of three types of RS-1 grounding cables to achieve the most efficient fuel consumption. The testing was conducted in two types: static and dynamic. Static testing is conducted on the engine at a certain rpm without applying load to the engine output. Dynamic testing is conducted on the engine to reach a speed of 35 km/h under the load of the vehicle’s weight. The application of RS-1 branded grounding cables affects fuel efficiency during static testing by 10%; in addition, vehicle acceleration to peak speed also increases, thus fuel consumption from speed 0–35 km/h decreases with the highest reduction of 13%. evidence.title: Active Energy Management for Enhanced Engine Transient Operations
evidence.abstract: Combat aircraft often require the engine to accelerate as fast as possible in response to the demand of maneuvering. The engine acceleration rate, however, is limited by the compressor surge constraint, which prevents more fuel addition that, otherwise, could provide for higher net shaft torque, and thus, faster acceleration. This paper examines the idea of using the electric starter/generator (ES/G) system to provide additional net shaft torque during this critical phase of acceleration. The idea is examined by simulations using a quasi-one-dimensional dynamic compressor flow model coupled with a lumped combustor–turbine model. A notional single-spool turbojet with a low overall pressure ratio is modeled and simulated. Simulation results suggest that an ES/G, when used as an electric-assist motor during acceleration, can help the engine to accelerate roughly 11, 48, and 70% faster compared to the case without ES/G participation, by using electric power roughly equivalent to 0.1, 1, and 3% of full-speed fuel combustion power, respectively. Furthermore, the respective increase in the acceleration rate leads to an additional 19, 80, and 113% of propulsion impulse, respectively (i.e., thrust integrated over time), during the first 5 s following the acceleration command.

evidence.abstract: With the enhancement of thermodynamic cycle parameters and heat dissipation constraints in aero-engines, effective thermal management has become a critical challenge to ensure safe and stable engine operation. This study developed a transient temperature evaluation model applicable to the entire flight envelope, considering fluid–solid coupling heat transfer on both the main flow path and fuel systems. Firstly, the impact of heat transfer on the acceleration and deceleration performance of a low-bypass-ratio turbofan engine was analyzed. The results indicate that, compared to the conventional adiabatic model, the improved model predicts metal components absorb 4.5% of the total combustor energy during cold-state acceleration, leading to a maximum reduction of 1.42 kN in net thrust and an increase in specific fuel consumption by 1.18 g/(kN·s). evidence.title: An Engine-Speed Stability-Enhanced Energy Management Strategy Under Power Transients for Heavy-Duty Hybrid Electric Vehicles
evidence.abstract: In heavy-duty hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), the engine–generator system (EGS) serves as the dominant power source for propulsion, paired with a small-capacity battery. During vehicle climbing or acceleration, the demand power varies significantly. Sudden changes in demanded power cannot be buffered by the battery alone, and part of the transient power must be supplied by EGS. However, the mismatch between the fast response of generator and the sluggish dynamic of engine leads to engine-speed fluctuation or even flameout, affecting the normal operation of vehicle. Thus, ensuring the vehicle stable operation and economy is a challenge. This article proposes an energy management strategy (EMS) considering EGS speed stability under power transients for heavy-duty HEVs. First, the Lyapunov theory and the sums-of-squares (SOS) optimization is employed to derive the mathematical expression of the EGS speed stability boundary. Then, according to the characteristics of hybrid powertrains, the dynamic boundary constraints of generalized stability regions are derived. Also, a real-time iteration method for the equivalence factor (EF) is proposed, integrating the shooting method to achieve the precise control within the feasible range. Finally, the proposed strategy is validated through simulations and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) experiments. The results indicate rotational-speed stability is improved by 64.7% compared with the base strategy.

One strategy to address the scarcity of fossil fuel energy sources is to conduct research and development aimed at improving fuel consumption efficiency. The development for fuel efficiency involves optimizing the engine management system, particularly the ignition system, so that the fuel entering the combustion chamber can burn completely. This study employs an experimental method by modifying the installation of three types of RS-1 grounding cables to achieve the most efficient fuel consumption. The testing was conducted in two types: static and dynamic. Static testing is conducted on the engine at a certain rpm without applying load to the engine output. Dynamic testing is conducted on the engine to reach a speed of 35 km/h under the load of the vehicle’s weight. The application of RS-1 branded grounding cables affects fuel efficiency during static testing by 10%; in addition, vehicle acceleration to peak speed also increases, thus fuel consumption from speed 0–35 km/h decreases with the highest reduction of 13%. The application of the cable during the 2024 competition showed a performance increase of 70%, with the RS-1 grounding cable contributing 13% efficiency.
Keywords: Engine wiring system, Fuel efficiency, Grounding cable.

system.value: Active Energy Management for Enhanced Engine Transient Operations

abstract.value: Combat aircraft often require the engine to accelerate as fast as possible in response to the demand of maneuvering. The engine acceleration rate, however, is limited by the compressor surge constraint, which prevents more fuel addition that, otherwise, could provide for higher net shaft torque, and thus, faster acceleration. This paper examines the idea of using the electric starter/generator (ES/G) system to provide additional net shaft torque during this critical phase of acceleration. The idea is examined by simulations using a quasi-one-dimensional dynamic compressor flow model coupled with a lumped combustor–turbine model. A notional single-spool turbojet with a low overall pressure ratio is modeled and simulated. Simulation results suggest that an ES/G, when used as an electric-assist motor during acceleration, can help the engine to accelerate roughly 11, 48, and 70% faster compared to the case without ES/G participation, by using electric power roughly equivalent to 0.1, 1, and 3% of full-speed fuel combustion power, respectively. Furthermore, the respective increase in the acceleration rate leads to an additional 19, 80, and 113% of propulsion impulse, respectively (i.e., thrust integrated over time), during the first 5 s following the acceleration command.

system.value: Transient Temperature Evaluation and Thermal Management Optimization Strategy for Aero-Engine Across the Entire Flight Envelope

abstract.value: With the enhancement of thermodynamic cycle parameters and heat dissipation constraints in aero-engines, effective thermal management has become a critical challenge to ensure safe and stable engine operation. This study developed a transient temperature evaluation model applicable to the entire flight envelope, considering fluid–solid coupling heat transfer on both the main flow path and fuel systems. Firstly, the impact of heat transfer on the acceleration and deceleration performance of a low-bypass-ratio turbofan engine was analyzed. The results indicate that, compared to the conventional adiabatic model, the improved model predicts metal components absorb 4.5% of the total combustor energy during cold-state acceleration, leading to a maximum reduction of 1.42 kN in net thrust and an increase in specific fuel consumption by 1.18 g/(kN·s). Subsequently, a systematic evaluation of engine thermal management performance throughout the complete flight mission was conducted, revealing the limitations of the existing thermal management design and proposing targeted optimization strategies, including employing Cooled Cooling Air technology to improve high-pressure turbine blade cooling efficiency, dynamically adjusting low-pressure turbine bleed air to minimize unnecessary losses, optimizing fuel heat sink utilization for enhanced cooling performance, and replacing mechanical pumps with motor pumps for precise fuel supply control.

system.value: An Engine-Speed Stability-Enhanced Energy Management Strategy Under Power Transients for Heavy-Duty Hybrid Electric Vehicles

abstract.value: In heavy-duty hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), the engine–generator system (EGS) serves as the dominant power source for propulsion, paired with a small-capacity battery. During vehicle climbing or acceleration, the demand power varies significantly. Sudden changes in demanded power cannot be buffered by the battery alone, and part of the transient power must be supplied by EGS. However, the mismatch between the fast response of generator and the sluggish dynamic of engine leads to engine-speed fluctuation or even flameout, affecting the normal operation of vehicle. Thus, ensuring the vehicle stable operation and economy is a challenge. This article proposes an energy management strategy (EMS) considering EGS speed stability under power transients for heavy-duty HEVs. First, the Lyapunov theory and the sums-of-squares (SOS) optimization is employed to derive the mathematical expression of the EGS speed stability boundary. Then, according to the characteristics of hybrid powertrains, the dynamic boundary constraints of generalized stability regions are derived. Also, a real-time iteration method for the equivalence factor (EF) is proposed, integrating the shooting method to achieve the precise control within the feasible range. Finally, the proposed strategy is validated through simulations and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) experiments. The results indicate rotational-speed stability is improved by 64.7% compared with the base strategy.

One strategy to address the scarcity of fossil fuel energy sources is to conduct research and development aimed at improving fuel consumption efficiency. The development for fuel efficiency involves optimizing the engine management system, particularly the ignition system, so that the fuel entering the combustion chamber can burn completely. This study employs an experimental method by modifying the installation of three types of RS-1 grounding cables to achieve the most efficient fuel consumption. Dynamic testing is conducted on the engine to reach a speed of 35 km/h under the load of the vehicle’s weight. The application of RS-1 branded grounding cables affects fuel efficiency during static testing by 10%; in addition, vehicle acceleration to peak speed also increases, thus fuel consumption from speed 0–35 km/h decreases with the highest reduction of 13%. The application of the cable during the 2024 competition showed a performance increase of 70%, with the RS-1 grounding cable contributing 13% efficiency.

custody_records.raw_content: Combat aircraft often require the engine to accelerate as fast as possible in response to the demand of maneuvering. The engine acceleration rate, however, is limited by the compressor surge constraint, which prevents more fuel addition that, otherwise, could provide for higher net shaft torque, and thus, faster acceleration. This paper examines the idea of using the electric starter/generator (ES/G) system to provide additional net shaft torque during this critical phase of acceleration. The idea is examined by simulations using a quasi-one-dimensional dynamic compressor flow model coupled with a lumped combustor–turbine model. A notional single-spool turbojet with a low overall pressure ratio is modeled and simulated. Simulation results suggest that an ES/G, when used as an electric-assist motor during acceleration, can help the engine to accelerate roughly 11, 48, and 70% faster compared to the case without ES/G participation, by using electric power roughly equivalent to 0.1, 1, and 3% of full-speed fuel combustion power, respectively. Furthermore, the respective increase in the acceleration rate leads to an additional 19, 80, and 113% of propulsion impulse, respectively (i.e., thrust integrated over time), during the first 5 s following the acceleration command.

custody_records.raw_content: In heavy-duty hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), the engine–generator system (EGS) serves as the dominant power source for propulsion, paired with a small-capacity battery. During vehicle climbing or acceleration, the demand power varies significantly. Sudden changes in demanded power cannot be buffered by the battery alone, and part of the transient power must be supplied by EGS. However, the mismatch between the fast response of generator and the sluggish dynamic of engine leads to engine-speed fluctuation or even flameout, affecting the normal operation of vehicle. Thus, ensuring the vehicle stable operation and economy is a challenge. This article proposes an energy management strategy (EMS) considering EGS speed stability under power transients for heavy-duty HEVs. First, the Lyapunov theory and the sums-of-squares (SOS) optimization is employed to derive the mathematical expression of the EGS speed stability boundary. Then, according to the characteristics of hybrid powertrains, the dynamic boundary constraints of generalized stability regions are derived. Also, a real-time iteration method for the equivalence factor (EF) is proposed, integrating the shooting method to achieve the precise control within the feasible range. Finally, the proposed strategy is validated through simulations and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) experiments. The results indicate rotational-speed stability is improved by 64.7% compared with the base strategy.
